newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany may borrow more to fill budget gap.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany may borrow more to fill budget gap.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, trying to soften the blow of disastrous news on slumping tax revenue, said on Wednesday that the country would still qualify for the single European currency.
But he said the government might have to increase new borrowing for 1997 because of persistently high unemployment.

Government coalition sources told Reuters that tax revenues would be nearly 20 billion marks ($12 billion) less than expected in 1997, opening a huge budget hole and casting doubt on Germany's chances of qualifying for economic and monetary union (EMU).

The news was leaked as federal, state and central bank officials met private-sector advisers in the eastern town of Schwerin to compile tax revenue estimates. They will formally deliver the new tax estimate on Thursday.

The federal budget had foreseen a deficit of 53.4 billion marks, which would leave Germany in line with the EMU target laid down in the Maastricht Treaty. The tax estimate made six months ago forecast 1997 revenue of 822 billion marks.
Waigel said the government has a variety of measures on hand to fill the gaps.
"We will do everything we can to fulfil the Maastricht criteria and we will fulfil them," he told reporters. "We are prepared with a number of corresponding measures."
The euro is scheduled to be launched in 1999 by countries which this year meet the Maastricht targets including limits on budget deficits, public debt and inflation.

Waigel said the coalition "would do everything it could to avoid tax increases" to fill the budget hole. New borrowing on top of the 53.4 billion marks ($31 billion) in debt already included in the 1997 budget "cannot be ruled out", he added.
Asked by reporters if new debt was unavoidable, he said the high costs of supporting four million unemployed meant that new borrowing "would be a logicial consequence of the facts".

Waigel, speaking at a book presentation in Bonn, said that the government was also considering selling part of its 75 percent stake in telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom AG earlier than the originally planned date of 2000.

The $13 billion sale of an inital 25 percent in November had no impact on government finances as the revenues went to the company itself. "With the company's exquisite state of health a sale of shares would not be a problem," Waigel said.

But his comments on selling more of the government's Telekom shares sent a shiver through the Frankfurt bourse, knocking the 30-share DAX index down 21.46 points to 3,573.69. Telekom shares fell 2.3 percent to 39.20 marks.
A Reuters survey of 35 European economists published on Wednesday showed Germany was the only country failing to make progress on achieving the Maastricht targets.
"We expect a tax revenue shortfall this year and it will be difficult to implement further cuts given high levels of unemployment," said Gernot Nerb, senior economist at Salomon Brothers Germany.
Otto Lambsdorff, a leader of the centrist Free Democrats who share power with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, said his party would never accept tax increases to fill the budget gaps.

"The FDP will not accept tax increases...The missing money has to be saved in the current budget, if necessary with a spending freeze. A slightly higher increase in borrowing is better than tax increases," he said.
Wolfgang Gerhardt, chairman of the FDP, agreed. "That (tax increases) would be poison for the economy," he said.

In a separate magazine interview, Gerhardt said that the stability of the euro would not be considerably undermined if Germany's budget deficit slighly exceeded the Maastricht targets, a position Waigel has stridently rejected.
($ = 1.705 German Marks)
